claims.text: Increasing effective laser energy density during SLM of refractory HEAs will reduce undissolved high-melting constituents.
Increasing effective laser energy density will minimize cracking and porosity.
Increasing effective laser energy density will improve the dimensional precision of SLM-fabricated refractory-HEA parts.
Increasing effective laser energy density will improve the mechanical integrity of SLM-fabricated refractory-HEA parts.
Powder-bed laser processing can produce cracks and undissolved tungsten particles in alloys containing refractory elements.
The cited baseline defect population includes porosity.
Tungsten is particularly difficult to dissolve during laser powder-bed processing because it has the highest melting point among the alloy constituents discussed.
Optimizing laser power, scan speed, and hatch spacing to raise volumetric energy input will ensure complete melting and homogeneous elemental mixing.
Combining alloying elements with substantially different melting points promotes undissolved particles during laser powder-bed processing.
Linear energy densities near or below 2.83 J/mm constitute a defect-producing baseline for refractory-HEA SLM.
The high melting points of refractory HEAs create processing difficulties.
Higher laser energy density will produce a more uniform and fully melted microstructure with fewer undissolved particles, cracks, and pores.
Increasing laser energy density reduces residual stresses.
Increasing laser energy density promotes a finer and more homogeneous microstructure.
A finer and more homogeneous microstructure improves dimensional stability during solidification.
The intervention is expected to increase yield strength and ductility relative to the current process baseline.
Excessive laser energy may introduce keyholing, thermal distortion, or excessive residual stresses.
The optimum laser energy density will vary with HEA composition and machine setup.
